segments.en: A breadfruit is roasting on an open fire, its green skin turning black and crackly. Break it open and the inside is soft, steaming and a little like fresh bread. Here in Saint Vincent, it's served with fried jackfish, and it's the national dish.

That breadfruit has a story. In the seventeen nineties, Captain William Bligh sailed here from the South Pacific carrying breadfruit plants, and a tree said to have grown from one of them still stands in the Botanic Gardens in Kingstown, among the oldest gardens in the Americas.
The country is made of one large green island, Saint Vincent, and a long tail of smaller islands to the south, the Grenadines, scattered across the sea like stepping stones towards Grenada.

Saint Vincent is steep and wild, with black sand beaches, waterfalls and rainforest. At its northern end rises La Soufrière, an active volcano. It erupted in twenty twenty-one, and communities pulled together to recover.

Long ago, this was home to the Kalinago people, and later to the Garifuna, whose ancestors were both Indigenous islanders and Africans. They resisted colonial rule fiercely, and Garifuna communities today in Central America trace their roots back here.

The Grenadines are a different world. Bequia has a harbour full of sailing boats and a long tradition of boatbuilding. In the Tobago Cays, a protected marine park, you can snorkel over the reef alongside sea turtles.

Most Vincentians call themselves Vincies, and the national carnival is Vincy Mas, held in the early summer. Steel pan bands compete, calypsonians sing clever songs about everyday life, and the streets fill with feathers, sequins and dancing.

Every Christmas, there are also Nine Mornings. For nine days before Christmas, people wake before dawn to walk, sing carols, swim in the sea and gather in the streets for concerts, a tradition you won't find anywhere else.
People speak English and also Vincentian Creole, a lively, musical way of talking that mixes English with words from Africa, France and the Caribbean.
The capital, Kingstown, is a busy little port where ferries leave for the Grenadines, and its market bursts with bananas, nutmeg and mangoes from the island's rich volcanic soil.
Cricket brings people together on weekends, and so does a good lime, which is the Caribbean word for relaxing and chatting with friends.
Thank you for sailing through our islands with us. Keep hopping south along the Grenadines, and the spice island of Grenada will be waiting for you at the end of the chain.
